deep.reconstruction:
This page is not mathematics. It is an observing-log sheet: calibration and adjustment notes for a transit instrument (Passageninstrument), apparently at Göttingen. The next sheet contains thread-transit times of alpha Ursae Minoris (Polaris) at upper and lower culmination on 11 October. That pairing is the classical way to determine the instrument's azimuth and collimation.

(a) First block. 'Mittelfaden d. Passageninstruments ... v. Meridian um 0,457' says the middle thread stands off the meridian by 0.457. The unit is probably screw revolutions or seconds of time. The successive readings 1: 0.457, 2: 0.891, 3: 1.320 are cumulative: displacing by one, two and three steps. The differences are 0.434 and 0.429. The mean per step is 1.320/3 = 0.440 (this computation is mine; Riemann does not write it).

(b) Second block, apparently with the thread on the other side of the meridian (perhaps after reversing the instrument). The thread is off by 1.594. Cumulative readings are 1: 1.594, 2: 3.140, 3: 4.703. Riemann writes the mean per step, 4.703/3 = 1.5677, as 1.567.

(c) A partly illegible remark about the middle position in the field of view and the collimation error 'in der jetzigen Lage' (in the present position of the instrument). It gives a screw-revolution value of 0.90 in time, refined to 0.905, i.e. about 0.9 s of time per revolution.

My interpretation, not on the page: if a and b are the per-step means for the two positions, the reversal method gives a collimation-type quantity (a+b)/2 ≈ 1.003 and an offset (b−a)/2 ≈ 0.564, depending on sign conventions.

(d) Bottom. An angle 44°32' (or possibly 44°1'32''; the superscripts are unclear) is set beside the formula '90° + φ − δ + Coll.-fehl.'. This is the circle reading expected for a star of declination δ at latitude φ, plus the collimation error. Two further values follow: 91°27' and −39°55', with '−39°50'' and 'Collimationsfehler +4'.

The written values are consistent with 91°27' − 39°55' = 51°32'. This equals the latitude of Göttingen (51°31'48''), which suggests the bottom lines are circle readings reduced with φ ≈ 51°32'. A reading of −39°55' against an expected −39°50' would leave a few arc-minutes attributed to collimation, noted as '+4'. This interpretation is mine.
errors: Readings in the first block are not exact multiples of 0.457 (0.891 vs 0.914; 1.320 vs 1.371). This is consistent with measured cumulative readings, not an error, but the mean per step is 0.440, not 0.457.
No mathematical errors identifiable; the only explicit arithmetic, 4.703/3 = 1.567 (truncated from 1.5677), is correct.

results.what: Mean per-step thread displacement from cumulative micrometer readings (4.703/3 = 1.567)
results.modern_name: Micrometer screw calibration / averaging of thread displacement
results.usually_credited_to: standard 19th-century observational astronomy practice (Bessel, Gauss era)

results.what: Determination of collimation error of a transit instrument; circle reading 90°+φ−δ+collimation
results.modern_name: Transit-instrument reduction (collimation and azimuth corrections, Mayer/Bessel formulas)

deep.surprise_reason: Routine practical-astronomy observation and calibration notes (transit instrument, Polaris culminations), probably made at the Göttingen observatory. They have no mathematical novelty; their only interest is biographical evidence of Riemann doing observational work.

mean per step of the first block ≈ 0.440

transcription_corrections: The 'previous page' transcription is the same sheet as this page (the identical image), not a different page.
In the second block the mean '1,567' is written beside line 3 (4,703); it is the per-step mean 4.703/3.
The bottom angle '441,32' with superscripts 0 and 1 is most likely 44°32' (degree and minute marks written above), though 44°1'32'' cannot be ruled out.
The heading word read as 'scheinbar westlich/östlich' is uncertain in the image; the previous transcription's '(Fäden [?] verglichen [?])' is an alternative reading.
'Schwankungen' is more plausibly 'Schraubenumdrehung' (screw revolution) = 0.90 s in time, as in the previous-page transcription.
